title: Progressive discovery vs. monolithic context: tool search and when to use it
titleVi: Khám phá từng bước so với ngữ cảnh nguyên khối: tìm kiếm công cụ và khi nào nên dùng

units.text: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
What you will be able to do
Quantify the per-request cost of loading every tool definition up front, and name the tool count where selection accuracy starts to slip
Configure tool search with defer_loading and explain how tool_reference blocks bring deferred tools into context
Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH in the Agent SDK and predict when each value loads tools up front
Choose between a fixed tool set, tool search, Skills and a hybrid for a given agent, weighing search round-trips against context saved
Key concept
Progressive discovery

Only lightweight entry points stay in context, such as a search tool or a Skill's name and description. Full definitions and instructions load when a request needs them. A monolithic strategy does the opposite: it loads everything on every request, whether or not that request uses it.

What a monolithic tool set costs before any work starts

A monolithic context strategy puts every tool definition into the context window on every request. That is the baseline that progressive discovery is measured against. Tool definitions count toward the context window just as messages do. The full cost of carrying too many tools is covered in
Capability bloat: what too many tools cost

. The angle here is how large that fixed cost gets. A typical multiserver setup that connects GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk can use about 55k tokens on definitions before Claude does anything useful. The Agent SDK documentation gives a smaller rule of thumb: 50 tools can take 10–20K tokens.

Tokens are only half of the cost. Claude's ability to pick the right tool degrades once more than 30–50 tools are available at the same time. An agent that worked well with two MCP servers can start choosing the wrong tool after a third or fourth server is connected, even though no single tool changed. Context rot adds to this. As the token count grows, accuracy and recall both decline, so a large block of mostly unused definitions also makes everything else in the window harder to use.
On the exam
The number to remember for tool-selection accuracy is 30–50 tools loaded at once. Single-digit tool counts are well below it. Hundreds of tools are far past it.

A larger context window does not fix either problem. More room lets the 55k tokens fit, but it does not restore selection accuracy, and context rot gets worse as the window fills. What matters is how much is in context, not how much space is left over.
Checkpoint 1 of 9
Check yourself

An agent connected to GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk MCP servers loads every tool definition up front, which is about 55k tokens. Since the last two servers were added, it often calls the wrong tool. A teammate suggests switching to a model with a much larger context window. What happens?
Tool selection recovers, because the 30–50 tool limit applies to each MCP server separately and no single server exceeds it.
The definitions fit more easily, but selection accuracy stays degraded because the same large tool set is still loaded at once, and context rot still applies.
The 55k-token cost disappears, because tool definitions only count toward the context window once a tool is called.
Tool selection recovers, because the 55k tokens of definitions now take up a much smaller share of the window.

How tool search keeps deferred tools out of context

Tool search is the API's progressive-discovery mechanism for tools. It replaces the monolithic catalogue with a search step. Tool search typically cuts the definition footprint by over 85 percent, loading only the 3–5 tools a given request needs. Because Claude chooses from a short, relevant list, selection accuracy stays high even when the catalogue holds thousands of tools.
Tool search comes in two variants. With the regex variant (
), Claude writes regex patterns. With the BM25 variant (

), Claude writes natural-language queries. Both search tool names, descriptions, argument names and argument descriptions, so well-written descriptions are what make a tool findable. Turning tool search on in the Agent SDK with ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH
In the Agent SDK, tool search is set by the
environment variable, which you pass through the

option. On Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5 and later models, tool search is on by default. This matters when you connect a large MCP server: its tools are deferred automatically unless you choose otherwise. Each value decides whether definitions are deferred or loaded up front.
ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH values and what each one does
Value
Behavior
(unset)
Tool search on; definitions deferred. Falls back to loading up front on older models, a non-first-party ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, or a Microsoft Foundry deployment hosted on Azure
true
Keeps tool search on even with a non-first-party ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL; requests fail on proxies that don't support tool_reference blocks
auto
Activates only when deferrable definitions reach 10% of the model's context window; below that, everything loads up front
auto:N
Same as auto with a custom threshold; auto:5 activates at 5%
false
Off; all tool definitions loaded into context on every turn

turns the choice between strategies into a measured threshold. It counts the tokens in the deferrable definitions and compares the total with the model's context window. A small tool set therefore stays monolithic, and a growing one switches to search without a code change. A lower N switches sooner.
forces the monolithic strategy on every turn. In the SDK, a catalogue can hold up to 10,000 tools, and each search returns the five most relevant by default.
An agent sets ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH to auto and connects a single MCP server whose tools use 3% of the context window. Are those tools deferred?

Choosing progressive discovery or a fixed tool set

The rule of thumb is to load a small, frequently used tool set up front and to use progressive discovery for large or rarely used catalogues. The cost of tool search is latency: Claude needs one extra turn to look up a tool before calling it. In return, baseline context usage drops sharply. That trade pays off for toolsets of about 20 or more tools where most aren't needed on every turn. It does not pay off when every tool is used constantly.
Matching the loading strategy to the tool set
Situation
Strategy
Reason
A handful of tools, nearly all used on almost every request
Load all up front (no tool search)
A search round-trip would precede calls to tools Claude needs anyway, and little context is saved
Roughly 20+ tools, most idle on any given turn
Tool search with defer_loading on the long tail
Large cut in baseline context for one extra lookup turn
Large catalogue with a few heavy-use tools
Tool search, with the 3–5 most frequent tools non-deferred
Common calls skip the search; rare tools stay out of context
Large but fixed toolset across many requests
Prompt caching (alone or with tool search)
Reduces what you pay for repeated definitions, not how many tokens sit in context

Take an internal agent with seven tools, about 1,200 tokens of definitions, and nearly every tool used on every request. Deferring those tools would add a search before calls Claude was always going to make, to save tokens that barely register. Keep them all loaded. The guidance to keep the 3–5 most-used tools non-deferred points the same way: whenever a tool is likely to be needed, it belongs in context.

The 55k-token multiserver agent is the opposite case. Tool search is the fix there, because it is the only option that removes definitions from context. Prompt caching makes repeated definitions cheaper, but every token still sits in context and the agent still chooses among dozens of tools. Rewriting every description by hand shrinks the definitions somewhat, but it leaves the tool count as it was and makes search worse, because names and descriptions are exactly what the search matches against. The approaches can be combined: tool search keeps the set lean, and caching lowers the cost of what stays loaded.
On the exam

If the question describes a small set of tools that are all used constantly, the answer is to load them up front. If it describes a large, multi-server catalogue with a big token footprint, the answer is tool search. Prompt caching lowers cost but not context size, so it never solves context bloat on its own.
Exam traps
Prompt caching the tool definitions solves context bloat from a large multi-server catalogue.
Why is that wrong?
Deferring every tool is always the most efficient choice, even for a small set of tools that are all used constantly.
Why is that wrong?

An enterprise agent aggregates tool catalogs from GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, and Splunk MCP servers, and the combined tool definitions consume about 55,000 tokens before the agent does any work. Which strategy best addresses this context bloat?
Enable tool search so Claude discovers and loads only the three to five tools relevant to each request instead of loading every definition upfront.

Skills and hybrid loading as other forms of progressive discovery
Tool search is not the only way to load context on demand. Agent Skills do the same thing for instructions and reference material. Skills load in three levels, described in
Progressive disclosure in Skills (three loading levels)

: metadata at startup, then the SKILL.md body when the Skill triggers, then bundled files when they are read. What matters for this choice is the always-on cost. Each Skill keeps about 100 tokens of name and description in the system prompt, so many Skills can be installed without paying for content nobody is using.
Tool search and Skills solve different problems. Tool search defers tool schemas, and the API finds and expands them through

blocks. Skills defer know-how: workflows, schemas and scripts. Claude reads them from a filesystem with bash, and only a script's output enters context, never its code. A large catalogue of actions points to tool search. A large body of procedures and reference documents points to Skills. Skills need the code execution environment to work. Tool search needs a model that supports it, and Claude Opus 4.1 and earlier do not.

A hybrid often works best. Claude Code puts CLAUDE.md files into context up front and uses glob and grep to pull in other files only when they are needed. On-demand exploration has a cost of its own: it is slower than reading data that was retrieved in advance, and an agent with poor guidance can waste context on dead ends. So load what nearly every request needs, and defer the rest.
Apply it to your own work

Think of an agent you have built or used. Which of its tools or instructions are needed on almost every request, and which come up only now and then? Where would you draw the line between loading up front and loading on demand?

Each one has a written workflow, a reference schema and a validation script, but any single request uses only one or two of them.
